en.title: Modern industry
en.summary: Manufacturing, services and finance in a changing economy.

paragraphs: Economies change in structure, not only in size. This lesson describes how British and American industry has shifted from coal and steel to services and technology, and practises correlative conjunctions.

Until the 1970s, coal, steel, shipbuilding and textiles employed millions of British workers. Not only have most of these industries declined; the places that depended on them have also had to reinvent themselves. Today the largest part of the economy is services: finance, insurance, education, health, retail and creative industries. The City of London is one of the world's leading financial centres. Manufacturing has not disappeared, but it has changed: cars and aircraft are now built by smaller workforces, assisted by robots. Similar changes have affected the American Midwest, where the old industrial region became known as the Rust Belt, while states such as California and Texas have grown quickly.
**1. Not only... but also, both... and, neither... nor.** After a negative opening, the verb is inverted. See Introduction to Grammar: Sentence structure.

blocks.html:
PatternExample
not only + inversionNot only have industries declined, but places have also changed.
both... andBoth banking and tourism have grown.
neither... norNeither coal nor steel employs many people now.

paragraphs: **2. Nouns made from verbs describe trends.** Decline, growth and shift can all be nouns. See Introduction to Grammar: Substantives (nouns).

blocks.html:
VerbNounExample
declinea declinea decline in coal mining
growgrowthgrowth in services
shifta shifta shift to services

items: **Sector** is a part of the economy.
**Workforce** is the people employed by a company or in an industry.
**Reinvent oneself** means to become something new.

paragraphs: In former industrial towns, old factories and mills have often been turned into museums, flats or offices.
